title: Germanic & Slavic Languages
summary: German, Dutch, Swedish, Russian, Polish and Ukrainian. Case is the shared threshold: when nouns change form for their role in the sentence, word order loosens and endings carry the meaning.
sources: Durrell: Hammer's German Grammar and Usage
König & van der Auwera: The Germanic Languages

nodes.label: The Germanic Family
nodes.summary: English, German, Dutch and the Scandinavian languages share a Proto-Germanic ancestor.
nodes.check: English, German, Dutch and Swedish share an ancestor called what?

nodes.label: German: Basics & Pronunciation
nodes.summary: Regular spelling, umlauts and capitalised nouns.
nodes.outcome: Greet and introduce yourself in German.
nodes.check: How do you say 'good morning' in German?

nodes.label: German: The Four Cases
nodes.summary: Nominative, accusative, dative and genitive change articles and endings by a noun's role. Troublesome because English has almost lost its cases.
nodes.outcome: Choose the right article for each case.

nodes.label: "Gender follows the thing's sex"
nodes.summary: Das Mädchen (the girl) is neuter because of the diminutive -chen ending.
nodes.check: What is the grammatical gender of German 'das Mädchen' (the girl)?
nodes.answer: Neuter: the diminutive ending -chen makes nouns neuter.

nodes.label: German: Verb-Second Word Order
nodes.summary: The conjugated verb sits in second place in main clauses and goes to the end in subordinate clauses.
nodes.outcome: Build main and subordinate clauses with correct verb position.
nodes.check: In a German main clause, where does the conjugated verb go?
nodes.answer: In second position (V2), e.g. 'Heute gehe ich nach Hause'.

nodes.label: Dutch
nodes.summary: Between English and German: familiar vocabulary with German-like word order.
nodes.outcome: Read simple Dutch using English and German cognates.
nodes.check: How do you say 'thank you' in Dutch?
nodes.answer: Dank je (informal) or dank u (formal); also bedankt.

nodes.label: Swedish
nodes.summary: Pitch accent, suffixed definite articles and simple verb forms.
nodes.check: How do you say 'thank you' in Swedish?

nodes.label: The Slavic Family
nodes.summary: East, West and South Slavic languages; rich case systems and verbal aspect.
nodes.outcome: Place a Slavic language in its branch.
nodes.check: Russian, Polish, Czech and Ukrainian belong to which branch of Indo-European?

nodes.label: Reading Cyrillic
nodes.summary: 33 letters, many familiar from Greek and Latin, some false friends (Р = r, Н = n).
nodes.check: Read the Cyrillic word 'Москва'. Which city is it?

nodes.label: Russian: Basics
nodes.summary: Stress, vowel reduction and everyday phrases.
nodes.check: How do you say 'thank you' in Russian?

nodes.label: Russian: Verbal Aspect
nodes.summary: Most verbs come in pairs: imperfective for process or repetition, perfective for a completed whole.
nodes.outcome: Choose the right aspect in past and future.
nodes.check: Russian verbs come in pairs like читать / прочитать. What distinction do the two aspects express?
nodes.answer: Imperfective (ongoing or repeated action) versus perfective (a single completed action).

nodes.label: Polish
nodes.summary: Seven cases, consonant clusters and fixed penultimate stress.
nodes.outcome: Decline a Polish noun through its cases.
nodes.check: How many grammatical cases does Polish have?

nodes.label: Ukrainian
nodes.summary: An East Slavic language with its own Cyrillic letters (і, ї, є, ґ), grammar and literature.
nodes.outcome: Greet and thank in Ukrainian and read its distinctive letters.
nodes.check: How do you say 'thank you' in Ukrainian?

nodes.label: "Ukrainian is a dialect of Russian"
nodes.summary: Ukrainian is a separate East Slavic language, as distinct from Russian as Spanish is from Portuguese.
nodes.outcome: Explain why Ukrainian is a language, not a dialect.
nodes.check: Is Ukrainian a dialect of Russian?
nodes.answer: No: it is a separate East Slavic language with its own grammar, vocabulary and literature.
